conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been so nauseous all day. Started around 5 a.m. Then in the evening, I started vomiting nonstop and was sweating a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a little on the right side of my belly, but not too bad. Mostly just the nausea and throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your blood sugar when you came in—it was very high, 529. And we found ketones, which means you were in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that’s why I feel so awful. I took my Lantus the night before, but I couldn’t keep anything down today, so I didn’t take any insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Because of the DKA, you were transferred to the ICU for an insulin IV to bring your levels down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right… I remember getting that. My stomach’s been so bad for so long. Is it just my gastroparesis flaring again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely the main trigger. Your labs showed an anion gap of 28, which confirms DKA, and your lactate was high too, at 3.7. But we’re treating that with insulin and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure was really high too, wasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was up to the 180s. You said you take lisinopril but not metoprolol anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped metoprolol because it made me tired. But I still take lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Since you couldn’t eat at first, we gave you IV medications to control your blood pressure. Once you can eat, we’ll switch back to your usual pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I also couldn’t pee all day… that’s why they put in a catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had about 900 mL in your bladder. But no signs of infection, and you’ve been able to go on your own since then. We removed the catheter yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your anion gap has closed—down to 11 now—and your blood sugar is much better. The insulin drip is being stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I’m out of the woods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The DKA is resolved, yes. But your nausea and vomiting are still ongoing. We’re continuing your usual anti-nausea meds—domperidone, Zofran, and Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried so many things… erythromycin made me worse before. Is there anything else we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team is following you. They’ve suggested an outpatient EGD with possible Botox injections into your stomach to help with the gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard about that. Would that really help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help some patients reduce nausea and vomiting. It’s not permanent, but it might give you relief for a few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to try it, if my GI doctor thinks it’s right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed something—we saw you putting your finger in your throat and coughing hard before vomiting. Can you tell me about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… sometimes I feel like I need to get it over with. The nausea is so bad, I just want to vomit and be done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand it’s distressing. A social worker spoke with you yesterday—was that helpful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, she was kind. I just feel stuck in this cycle. Every time I get sick, I end up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. The good news is your labs are improving. Your lactate is down to 1.0, and your kidneys are fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re starting to advance your diet—clear liquids first, then soft foods if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous… I haven’t kept anything down in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. Small sips. And we’ll keep your anti-nausea meds going around the clock for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor? I had some apple juice and crackers… and I kept them down!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent! That’s a big step forward. Let’s try a soft meal later and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’ve been tolerating regular food, your blood sugars are stable on subcutaneous insulin, and your vitals are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow or the day after. We’ll make sure you’re steady on your feet and managing meals first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on the same insulin as before—28 units Lantus at supper, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And Humalog as needed with meals, based on your blood sugar. We’ll send that home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds—lisinopril and metoprolol—both again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your pressure has been well-controlled since switching back to oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s blood sugar was 98, and your morning labs look great. You’re on track for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. What about the EGD with Botox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set up a referral to your GI doctor. They’ll decide if it’s right for you and schedule it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start vomiting again at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your anti-nausea meds as prescribed. If you can’t keep fluids down, or your blood sugar goes very high, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. You’re going home with the same meds, no changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll schedule that. And your primary care doctor too. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to say thanks again. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. Keep up with your insulin and diet, and take your anti-nausea meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been writing down my blood sugars. Is that helpful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. It helps you and your doctors see patterns. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Rest, stay hydrated, and follow up with your GI doctor about the EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I wear my scopolamine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue it every 72 hours as before. It may help with nausea, especially if you’re traveling or feeling unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take it easy and keep in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve packed up. Ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Discharge papers are signed. You’re officially going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care of yourself.
